card.title: THE LAND GIRLS
card.flavorText: First created in 1917, the Women’s Land Army (WLA) was reformed in 1939 to safeguard British food production as war was imminent. With the regular agricultural workforce depleted by military conscription, the government turned to women to keep farms running. By 1944, the WLA had grown to nearly 80,000 members, nicknamed “Land Girls”. Recruits came from all backgrounds, including cities, and underwent short training courses before being assigned to farms across Britain. Their tasks were varied and often strenuous: cultivating crops, managing livestock, maintaining machinery, and even felling trees. Pay was low and the work physically demanding, yet Land Girls quickly proved their value, earning respect from initially doubtful farmers. Many lived on-site in hostels or with farming families. Despite limited comforts, the WLA fostered strong morale through shared purpose and the novelty of rural life. The government supported recruitment with posters and films showing Land Girls as patriotic heroines vital to the war effort. Their contribution was crucial in avoiding severe food shortages during the war.
